title: The priest in the tree
translation: I went to see the horse races at Kamo in early summer. A crowd of common people stood in front of our carriage and we couldn't see a thing, so we all got down and went up to the fence. But it was packed there too, and there was no way to squeeze through.

Then I noticed a priest who had climbed a chinaberry tree across the way and settled into a fork in the branches to watch. He was holding on, but he kept dozing off, and every time he was about to fall, he woke up with a start. The people watching him jeered. "What an idiot! Up on a branch like that, and sleeping as if he didn't have a care in the world."
Something occurred to me, and I said it out loud: "Any of us could die right now. We forget that and spend the whole day watching the races. That's even more foolish."
The people in front of me said, "You're quite right, sir. We're the real fools." They all turned round, said "Please, come through here", made room and let me in.
Anyone could have thought of something that obvious. Maybe, at that moment, it caught them off guard and hit home. People aren't made of wood or stone. At the right moment, something gets through.

literal: When I watched the Kamo horse race on the fifth day of the fifth month, common people stood in front of the carriage blocking it and we could not see, so each of us got down and went up to the edge of the fence, but especially many people were crowded there, and there was no way to push in.
At such a moment, there was a priest who had climbed a chinaberry tree opposite and sat in the fork of the tree, watching.
While clinging on, he slept deeply, and many times, when he was about to fall, he woke up.
The people who saw this jeered in amazement: 'What a fool of the world! On such a dangerous branch, he must be sleeping with an easy mind', they said, and
as it had just come into my mind, I said, 'The coming of our death may be right now. Forgetting this and spending the day watching things: the foolishness is even greater', and
the people in front said, 'Truly, it is just so. We are most foolish', and all looked back and said, 'Please come here', and gave up their place and called me in.
Such a principle: who would not think of it? But perhaps, at that moment, it felt unexpected and struck their hearts.
Since people are not wood and stone, it is not that they are never moved by things, depending on the moment.

notes.text: The horse race at the Kamo shrine (Kamigamo), held on the fifth day of the fifth month, around early summer. Pairs of riders race along a straight track. It is still held every year on 5 May. {競馬|くらべうま}: 'comparing horses'; modern {競馬|けいば} is the same word read in Sino-Japanese.
{埒|らち}: the fence along the track (see section 150 for the horse image). Modern {埒|らち}があかない, 'to get nowhere', comes from the same word.
{楝|あふち}: the chinaberry tree (modern センダン), which flowers pale purple in early summer, just at the time of the race.
しれもの: 'fool, idiot'. {世|よ}の … : 'the greatest … in the world'. The crowd is enjoying itself.
らむ: a guess about something happening right now, 'he must be sleeping'.

notes.quote: 我等が生死の到来唯今にもやあらむ
notes.text: {生死|しやうじ}: in Buddhist language 'birth and death', here simply death. や … む: 'might it be…?'. The same thought as the end of section 137, which is also set among the crowds at a Kamo festival.
The common people answer in polite {候|さうら}ふ style. They speak to Kenkō politely, as to a priest and a gentleman. けれ: けり of realisation, 'so it is'.
き: the past of personal experience. Kenkō was there, and he got his good place.

'People are not wood or stone': from a line by the Chinese poet Bai Juyi (772–846), in his poem 'Lady Li': 'people are not wood or stone, they all have feelings'. It was a common saying in Kenkō's time.
